clue.text: Officers have two keys' of the old, prison

parts.note: marshals are officers of law or ceremony
E is one musical key
A is a second musical key

explanation.surface: Prison officers carry a pair of keys to the cells of an old jail.
explanation.walkthrough: Musical keys are named by letters A to G, so 'two keys' supplies two of those letters, E and A. The Marshalsea was a notorious debtors' prison in Southwark, London, closed in 1842.
explanation.definitionFit: The Marshalsea was a historic London jail, famous from Dickens's Little Dorrit.

clue.text: A cigar manufactured from fungus

indicators.note: something manufactured is made up, so the letters are assembled anew

explanation.surface: A cheroot rolled from mushroom matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Manufactured' rearranges A CIGAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Agaric is a gilled mushroom, such as the fly agaric.

clue.text: It might give way to road transport

definitions.text: It might give way to road transport

parts.words: It might give way to road transport
parts.note: read not as yielding to traffic but as showing travellers the route to take

explanation.walkthrough: 'Give way' looks like the road instruction to yield, but it means show the way.
explanation.definitionFit: A roadside pointer indicates directions to motorists.

clue.text: A highly entertaining person

parts.note: read literally: someone who entertains guests while high in the sky

explanation.walkthrough: 'Highly' means at altitude, not very; the person looks after passengers on a plane.
explanation.definitionFit: A stewardess on an aircraft hosts passengers aloft.

clue.text: A derisive glutton ?

explanation.definitionFit: To scoff is both to mock and to eat greedily, so one who does either fits both senses.

clue.text: A runner for the county

definitions.meaning: a former English county around Bristol and Bath

explanation.definitionFit: Avon is the name of several English rivers and of a county that existed from 1974 to 1996.

clue.text: Late issue of notes-going up to 27 ?

definitions.text: Late issue of notes-going up to 27 ?

parts.words: Late issue of notes-going up to 27 ?
parts.note: music played in the evening, sent up beneath a beloved's window

explanation.walkthrough: 'Late issue of notes' is not a delayed banknote printing but night-time music; 27 refers to the beloved in 27 across.
explanation.definitionFit: Evening music sung or played by a lover outside his beloved's window.

clue.text: Longfellow's landlord told of his midnight ride

definitions.text: Longfellow's landlord told of his midnight ride

parts.words: Longfellow's landlord told of his midnight ride
parts.note: in Longfellow's Tales of a Wayside Inn, the Landlord's Tale is a poem about a famous night ride

explanation.walkthrough: The Landlord's Tale in Longfellow's collection is the poem about the patriot who rode to warn of British troops in 1775.
explanation.definitionFit: The American silversmith whose night gallop warned colonists is the hero of that tale.

clue.text: Jeeves goes to a dance (for a spell)

parts.note: Jeeves is the gentleman's gentleman, or valet, in P. G. Wodehouse's stories

explanation.surface: The famous butler-figure slips out to a ball for a short while.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeeves, Bertie Wooster's manservant in Wodehouse, is a crossword stand-in for any valet. The bracketed 'for a spell' only colours the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The valeta is an old-time round ballroom routine in waltz time.

clue.text: Beast takes the final blow without a tortured groan

indicators.note: used in its old sense of outside: the knockout letters sit around the rest

parts.note: KO, a knockout, is the blow that ends a boxing match

indicators.note: tortured sits amid the words a and groan, which are twisted into a new order as if wrenched in pain

explanation.surface: An animal receives the deathblow, never letting out an agonised moan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' here means 'outside', so the letters of KO go round ANGARO, the anagram of A GROAN signalled by 'tortured'.
explanation.definitionFit: A kangaroo is an Australian marsupial, an animal or creature.

clue.text: Some merriment before the French turn dismal

parts.note: fun is a measure of merriment or amusement
ere is a poetic word meaning before

indicators.note: the French article is turned round so it reads from right to left

parts.note: la is the feminine form of the in French

explanation.surface: Gaiety comes first, then the French grow gloomy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn' reverses LA to AL at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Funereal means suited to a burial, hence gloomy and sombre.

clue.text: " The cave where lies" (R and J)

definitions.text: " The cave where lies" (R and J)

parts.words: " The cave where lies" (R and J)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Romeo and Juliet: Juliet speaks of tearing the cave where the mythical nymph who repeats voices lies

explanation.walkthrough: In the balcony scene Juliet says she would 'tear the cave where Echo lies'; the nymph Echo pined away until only her voice remained.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is the nymph of Greek myth who could only repeat others' words, whose name also means a reflected sound.

clue.text: They look out for The Corsair in revised texts

indicators.note: the pirate goes inside the reworked letters
revised text is altered, so the letters of texts are reordered

parts.note: a rover is a pirate or corsair

explanation.surface: Readers on the lookout for Byron's poem in new editions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revised' reorders TEXTS as EXT...TS, and 'in' puts ROVER inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Outgoing people direct their interest outward, as opposed to introspective types.

clue.text: Ass kept dithering about little gamble

indicators.note: the jumbled letters are placed around the other piece
dithering suggests shaky indecision, so the letters of ass and kept are jumbled

parts.note: wee is Scottish for small

explanation.surface: A fool hesitates over whether to place a small bet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dithering' gives SPSTAKE (an anagram of ASS KEPT), and 'about' puts it round WEE, splitting it after the first S.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweepstake is a lottery-style bet where the pooled stakes go to the winners.

clue.text: Churchman is for trial, with hill-dweller

parts.note: pro is Latin for in favour of
a test is a trial
an ant lives in an anthill

explanation.surface: A clergyman supports the experiment alongside a mountain resident.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hill-dweller' wants a highlander, but it is the insect of the anthill.
explanation.definitionFit: A Protestant is a member of a reformed Western church.

clue.text: Job for a horse

parts.note: read as a role a horse might fill: one bred to race at a particular gait in harness

explanation.walkthrough: A trotter is a horse trained for harness racing at the trot; the word also means a pig's foot.
explanation.definitionFit: The horse whose work is trotting in harness races takes its name from that gait.

clue.text: Barely surpass the others ?

parts.note: read as beating everyone at undressing, being more bare than the rest

explanation.walkthrough: 'Barely' suggests by a whisker, but the pun is on stripping more than everyone else.
explanation.definitionFit: To outstrip is to outdo or overtake.

clue.text: Figure about a month back shows yield

indicators.note: the figure goes around the other piece

parts.note: a cone is a solid geometrical figure

indicators.note: the month's abbreviation is read backwards

parts.note: Dec is the short form of December

explanation.surface: A number taken from about a month ago shows the harvest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' turns DEC into CED, which 'about' sets inside CONE after CON.
explanation.definitionFit: To concede is to give in or surrender, the verb sense of yield.

clue.text: Our course is clear here

parts.note: course means a dish at dinner and clear describes a thin, strained soup

explanation.walkthrough: 'Course' and 'clear' sound like navigation, but describe a clear soup served as a course.
explanation.definitionFit: A clarified meat broth served as a starter.

clue.text: Poem and song to note'

parts.note: a ballad is a narrative song
E is a musical note

explanation.surface: Verse set to music, down to the last note.
explanation.walkthrough: The ballade is a French verse form of three stanzas and an envoi.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballade is a fixed form of verse with a refrain.

clue.text: Where we might find star 'parts for US opera, etc

indicators.note: parts as a verb means splits up, so the letters are broken and rearranged

explanation.surface: Casting notes on roles for an American opera and the like.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parts' breaks up US OPERA and ETC to give the ten letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Stars lie in the void beyond Earth's atmosphere.

clue.text: Cannot easily part with money

indicators.note: only a part of the words cannot easily is taken, a run of letters inside them

explanation.surface: Someone reluctant to hand over cash.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'canNOT Easily'.
explanation.definitionFit: A banknote is paper currency.

clue.text: Muscle demands rest-no twisting

indicators.note: twisting distorts the order, so the letters of rest and no are rearranged

explanation.surface: A strained muscle needs a break, and no wrenching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twisting' rearranges REST and NO.
explanation.definitionFit: A tensor is a muscle that tightens or stretches a body part.

clue.text: At the outside, East gets a £10 rent change

parts.note: E is the compass abbreviation for east

indicators.note: the letters are changed into a new order

parts.note: the pound sign stands for L (from Latin libra) and 10 is the Roman numeral X

explanation.surface: An Eastern tenant has a ten-pound rise in the rent.
explanation.walkthrough: £ gives L and 10 the Roman X; 'change' turns A, L, X and RENT into XTERNAL after E.
explanation.definitionFit: External means on the outer side, outward.

clue.text: Crackers for them

parts.note: crackers are tools for opening shells, and crackers also means mad

explanation.walkthrough: Nutcrackers exist for these, and 'crackers' is British slang for mad, which is what this word means too.
explanation.definitionFit: The shelled fruits that nutcrackers open; also slang for crazy.

clue.text: Scare-monger makes a number prepare to fight — it's wrong

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral fifty
to arm is to make ready for battle

indicators.note: the letters of it's are put in a wrong order

explanation.surface: A doom-monger rallies a crowd to battle, though it's a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrong' turns IT'S into IST to finish.
explanation.definitionFit: An alarmist is someone who spreads needless panic.

clue.text: The right bracket.?

parts.note: plays on the saying 'as right as' a three-legged stand, and on a bracket as a support rather than a typographic mark

explanation.walkthrough: 'As right as a trivet' is an old British idiom for perfectly fine; a trivet is a metal stand or bracket for a pot.
explanation.definitionFit: A trivet is a small metal stand set beside a fire to hold a kettle, a kind of support.

clue.text: A lover of course and hater, possibly

parts.note: the sweet is the dessert course of a meal

indicators.note: possibly signals that hater is just one arrangement of these letters

explanation.surface: Someone who is a romantic, naturally, but could equally be full of loathing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' rearranges HATER into HEART.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweetheart is a beloved partner or darling.
